title: Who Is Vishal Sikka? The AI Pioneer Who Ran Infosys — and Just Raised $85 Million to Disrupt It
excerpt: Nine years after a bruising exit from Infosys, the 59-year-old former SAP CTO has founded Hang Ten Systems, an enterprise AI startup that closed $85 million in seed funding in four months — with Intel and Micron's CEOs writing checks.
body:
On September 16, 2026, a four-month-old startup with about two dozen employees announced it had raised another $53 million. That took Hang Ten Systems' total seed funding to $85 million — an extraordinary sum for a company barely old enough to have a lease. But Hang Ten is not a typical seed-stage bet. Its founder is Vishal Sikka: the man who once ran Infosys, helped create SAP HANA, and was an early adviser to OpenAI.

The round, led by Temasek's early-stage platform Xora, closed just five weeks after an initial $32 million seed led by Mayfield. The cap table reads like a who's who of the chip and internet eras: Aramco Ventures, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, and Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang, who also sits on the board.

Shajapur to Stanford

Vishal Sikka was born on May 1, 1967, in Shajapur, a small town in Madhya Pradesh, to Punjabi parents — his father an officer in the Indian Railways, his mother a teacher. When he was six, the family moved to Vadodara in Gujarat, where he attended Kendriya Vidyalaya in Rajkot and Rosary High School in the city.

He enrolled in computer engineering at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda but left midway, bound for Syracuse University in New York, where he earned a B.S. in computer science. Then came Stanford, where he completed his PhD in 1996 under adviser Michael Genesereth. But the more telling detail is who opened the door: Marvin Minsky, one of the founding fathers of artificial intelligence, wrote Sikka's recommendation letter for Stanford. John McCarthy, another father of AI, was one of his professors.

The man who built HANA — and ran Infosys

After a stint at Xerox's research labs and two startups of his own — iBrain, acquired by PatternRX, and Bodha.com, acquired by Peregrine Systems — Sikka joined SAP in 2002. In April 2007 he became SAP's first-ever chief technology officer, and later joined the executive board. His signature achievement was SAP HANA, the in-memory database platform he spearheaded with co-founder Hasso Plattner's backing — the foundation of SAP's entire product line.

In June 2014, Infosys named Sikka its CEO and managing director, the first person from outside the founding team to lead the company. He took over on August 1, 2014, from co-founder S.D. Shibulal, promising to drag the services giant into the age of AI and automation. In December 2015, he pledged Infosys's support to a newly formed nonprofit AI research lab called OpenAI, and was listed as an adviser.

It ended badly. In August 2017, after months of public sparring with co-founder N.R. Narayana Murthy over corporate governance and executive pay, Sikka resigned. It was a bruising, very public fall for one of the most powerful executives in Indian tech; India Today had ranked him 32nd among the country's 50 most powerful people that year.

The $85 million second act

Sikka did not stay down. In 2019 he founded Vianai Systems, an enterprise AI company that raised $50 million in initial funding and later $140 million in a round led by SoftBank's Vision Fund 2. He joined Oracle's board of directors in December 2019, the BMW Group's supervisory board, and became an adviser to Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI.

This April, he quietly left Vianai. A month later, he founded Hang Ten Systems in Palo Alto. The name comes from "hang ten," the surfing maneuver in which a rider plants all ten toes over the front of the board — for Sikka, a metaphor for riding what he calls "probably the biggest wave of our lives."

Hang Ten's pitch is simple: AI has collapsed the cost of building software, so the scarcest resource is no longer code but trusted partners who can define requirements and validate that systems actually work. The startup advises companies with over $10 billion in annual revenue on AI strategy and builds their software with an in-house framework, Hobie, that packages reusable AI "skills" for regulated industries — promising customers a tenfold improvement in cost, speed, or both.

The thesis is landing. Within 25 days of a first meeting, Hang Ten signed a multimillion-dollar contract to build a mission-critical system — "I had never seen enterprise deals move that quickly," Sikka told TechCrunch. The company now works with 21 major enterprises across the U.S., Europe, the Middle East and Asia, including Fresenius Kabi, Saudi Aramco and Siemens Energy, and has turned down acquisition offers from "very big companies."

"We are fortunate that we don't have the burden of legacy that we have to transform."

That line — Sikka's answer when asked how a startup like Hang Ten could disrupt services giants like Infosys — carries the whole story.

The diaspora arc

Sikka's career traces the classic Indian-diaspora arc in technology, but with unusual symmetry: a boy from Shajapur and Vadodara, mentored by the founders of AI at Stanford, who went on to lead two of the largest enterprise software institutions on two continents — SAP in Germany, Infosys in India — and is now, at 59, founding startups in Silicon Valley at the exact moment AI becomes the biggest wave of our lives.

Nine years after the Infosys exit that many assumed would define him, the $85 million bet on Hang Ten suggests the defining chapter may be the one he is writing now.
image_caption: Vishal Sikka speaking at SAP's SAPPHIRE conference in Orlando in 2010, when he was the company's first-ever CTO. In 2026 he founded Hang Ten Systems, an enterprise AI startup that has raised $85 million in seed funding.
nri_angle: Sikka's arc — small-town Madhya Pradesh to Stanford mentorship under AI's founding fathers to the top of Infosys and SAP, and now a founder again at 59 — embodies the Indian diaspora's outsize role in the AI era.
author: Diaspora Desk
